Therefore, hydrogen output from production must be liquefied before end use. To liquefy hydrogen, gaseous hydrogen is first compressed and precooled, typically using liquid nitrogen at about −196°C (77 K). This step is followed by cryogenic cooling using heat exchangers and a Joule-Thomson expansion, which drops the temperature of the hydrogen below its boiling point of −253°C (20 K), thus liquefying the hydrogen (Züttel 2003; Al Ghafri et al. 2022). Any hydrogen that remains in a cold vapor phase after the Joule-Thomson expansion is fed back to the precooling step to help further lower the temperature of the hydrogen (Chart Industries n.d.-a). As noted in Table 8, electricity input for liquefaction ranges from 8 kWh/kg to 15 kWh/kg, which is 24% to 45% of the lower heating value of hydrogen (33.3 kWh/kg) (Gardiner 2009; Al Ghafri et al. 2022). Research indicates energy input for liquefaction could drop below 8 kWh/kg, with a theoretical limit of about 3 kWh/kg (Gardiner 2009; Al Ghafri et al. 2022; Washington State University n.d.). Hydrogen liquefaction is an established commercial technology with considerable technology deployment during the 1950s and 1960s in the United States to support the NASA space program. As of May 2024, the United States had 14 plants in operation with a total existing and planned hydrogen liquefaction capacity of 794 MTPD. Each operating plant has a capacity between 5 MTPD and 32 MTPD. The largest planned hydrogen liquefaction facility in the United States has a capacity of 90 MTPD (Wieliczko 2024). 4.1.2 Hydrogen General Distribution Methods As of 2025, almost all hydrogen production is colocated with or located nearby (just beyond the gate of) demand. This is primarily due to the low (volumetric) energy density of hydrogen, which has negative impacts on transport costs and logistics. These negative impacts have hindered investment in delivery infrastructure. The few hydrogen delivery technologies that are commercially deployed as of 2025 include gaseous trucking, gaseous pipelines, and liquid hydrogen trucking. Gaseous and liquid trucking options are largely dedicated to providing hydrogen for small demand nodes, such as refueling stations and specialty applications, where having a dedicated production facility would not be economically viable. Of the two trucking options, vacuum- insulated liquid hydrogen tanker trucking, with approximately 3,800-kg H carrying capacity per 2 truck (Argonne National Laboratory n.d.), would be more viable for airport deliveries, especially in the near term as hydrogen-fueled aircraft reach the market and airport LH demand is limited. 2 Compressed gaseous hydrogen trucking to airports, with less than 1,000-kg H carrying capacity 2 per truck (DOE n.d.-g), would be impractical in the near term because hydrogen would need to be liquefied at the airport, losing the economies-of-scale benefit of centralized liquefaction. Additionally, a liquid hydrogen tanker truck costs around $1–$2 million, and a gaseous tube trailer truck is roughly $1 million as of 2025 (Argonne National Laboratory n.d.; Munster 2025).
